def:
The configuration state that turns raw MMIO offsets and TLP fields into NVMe meaning: BAR0 base, doorbell stride (CAP.DSTRD), queue base addresses and sizes, and the MSI-X vector of each completion queue. A capture that starts after this was set up cannot be decoded with certainty.
Common confusion: decoding doorbell offsets with an assumed stride of 4 bytes.

Reconstructing missing binding context (queue addresses, stride, vectors) from traffic patterns when the capture lacks the setup commands. Conclusions drawn from it carry lower confidence and must be labelled as inferred.
Common confusion: presenting inferred queue mapping as observed fact.

The time an NVMe command spends between consecutive observable events on the link: doorbell write, SQE fetch, data transfer, CQE write and interrupt. It shows which stage (host, controller or link) takes the time.
Common confusion: treating total command latency as one number without stages.

TLPs that crossed the link but are missing from an analyzer capture, for example because a buffer overflowed or a filter or trigger window was wrong. Gaps in Data Link Layer sequence numbers reveal it.
Common confusion: concluding that a device never sent a TLP the analyzer failed to record.

Data a device read that does not match what the host intended at that moment, such as an SQE fetched before the host's write became visible because a memory barrier was missing before the doorbell.
Common confusion: blaming the controller for executing the wrong command.

An explicit statement of how surely a TLP or event is tied to a particular NVMe command (high, medium or low), based on the identifiers that link them: CID, queue, address and timing.
Common confusion: matching by timing alone and reporting it as certain.

Bit 15 of Get Log Page CDW10. When set, reading the log does not clear the asynchronous event that pointed to it, so events of that type stay masked until a read with RAE cleared.
Common confusion: monitoring agents that read with RAE=1 and then never receive another event.

A burst of host retries that keeps a failing or busy controller overloaded, often because Command Retry Delay or DNR was ignored or because all retries happen at the same time.
Common confusion: adding more retries to fix a problem that retries are making worse.

Field in an Error Information log entry that gives the byte and bit of the command that the controller rejected. It points to the bad field in an Invalid Field in Command error.
Common confusion: expecting every controller to fill it in; FFFFh means not available.

The part a PCIe function played in a failed transaction: receiver, transmitter, requester, completer or intermediate (switch). It decides which function logs which error. The function that logs an error is often not the one that caused it.
Common confusion: assuming the reporter is the cause.

The PCI Express Base Specification's rules that make a function report only the most significant error when one event triggers several, so that one fault does not produce a misleading cascade of errors.
Common confusion: concluding that secondary conditions did not occur because their status bits are clear.

A link that, after Recovery or retraining, runs at a lower speed or width than both ends support. You can see it by comparing Link Status with Link Capabilities. It usually lowers the error rate and hides a problem with signal margin.
Common confusion: missing it because I/O still works.
